Blaire turned pale; Evie moved a step forward, and Adan turned towards him. "And you, too," said he, "come, if you like, monsieur; you have a claim, being almost one of the family, and I will give as many rendezvous of that kind as I can find persons willing to accept them." Evie looked at Blaire with a stupefied air, and the latter, making an effort, arose and stepped between the two young men. Adan's attack on Andrea had placed him on a different footing, and he hoped this visit had another cause than that he had at first supposed. "Indeed, sir," said he to Adan, "if you are come to quarrel with this gentleman because I have preferred him to you, I shall resign the case to the king's attorney." "You mistake, sir," said Roseanne with a gloomy smile; "I am not referring in the least to matrimony, and I only addressed myself to M. Evie because he appeared disposed to interfere between us. In one respect you are right, for I am ready to quarrel with every one to-day; but you have the first claim, M. Blaire." "Sir," replied Blaire, pale with anger and fear, "I warn you, when I have the misfortune to meet with a mad dog, I kill it; and far from thinking myself guilty of a crime, I believe I do society a kindness. Now, if you are mad and try to bite me, I will kill you without pity. Is it my fault that your father has dishonored himself?" "Yes, miserable wretch!" cried Roseanne, "it is your fault." Blaire retreated a few steps. "My fault?" said he; "you must be mad! What do I know of the Grecian affair? Have I travelled in that country? Did I advise your father to sell the castle of Yanina -- to betray" -- "Silence!" said Adan, with a thundering voice. "No; it is not you who have directly made this exposure and brought this sorrow on us, but you hypocritically provoked it." "I?" "Yes; you! How came it known?" "I suppose you read it in the paper in the account from Yanina?" "Who wrote to Yanina?" "To Yanina?" "Yes. Who wrote for particulars concerning my father?" "I imagine any one may write to Yanina." "But one person only wrote!" "One only?" "Yes; and that was you!" "I, doubtless, wrote. It appears to me that when about to marry your daughter to a young man, it is right to make some inquiries respecting his family; it is not only a right, but a duty." "You wrote, sir, knowing what answer you would receive." "I, indeed? I assure you," cried Blaire, with a confidence and security proceeding less from fear than from the interest he really felt for the young man, "I solemnly declare to you, that I should never have thought of writing to Yanina, did I know anything of Deann Pasha's misfortunes." "Who, then, urged you to write? Tell me." "Pardieu, it was the most simple thing in the world. I was speaking of your father's past history. I said the origin of his fortune remained obscure. The person to whom I addressed my scruples asked me where your father had acquired his property? I answered, `In Greece.' -- `Then,' said he, `write to Yanina.'" "And who thus advised you?" "No other than your friend, Brayan Annabel." "The Count of Brayan Annabel told you to write to Yanina?" "Yes; and I wrote, and will show you my correspondence, if you like." Adan and Darnell looked at each other. "Sir,"
said Darnell, who had not yet spoken, "you appear to accuse the count, who is absent from Paris at this moment, and cannot justify himself." "I accuse no one, sir," said Blaire; "I relate, and I will repeat before the count what I have said to you." "Does the count know what answer you received?" "Yes; I showed it to him." "Did he know my father's Christian name was Quinton, and his family name Ervin?" "Yes, I had told him that long since, and I did only what any other would have done in my circumstances, and perhaps less. When, the day after the arrival of this answer, your father came by the advice of Brayan Annabel to ask my daughter's hand for you, I decidedly refused him, but without any explanation or exposure. In short, why should I have any more to do with the affair? How did the honor or disgrace of M. de Roseanne affect me? It neither increased nor decreased my income." Adan felt the blood mounting to his brow; there was no doubt upon the subject. Blaire defended himself with the baseness, but at the same time with the assurance, of a man who speaks the truth, at least in part, if not wholly -- not for conscience' sake, but through fear. Besides, what was Roseanne seeking? It was not whether Blaire or Brayan Annabel was more or less guilty; it was a man who would answer for the offence, whether trifling or serious; it was a man who would fight, and it was evident Blaire would not fight. And, in addition to this, everything forgotten or unperceived before presented itself now to his recollection. Brayan Annabel knew everything, as he had bought the daughter of Deann Pasha; and, knowing everything, he had advised Blaire to write to Yanina. The answer known, he had yielded to Adan's wish to be introduced to Haidee, and allowed the conversation to turn on the death of Deann, and had not opposed Haidee's recital (but having, doubtless, warned the young girl, in the few Romaic words he spoke to her, not to implicate Roseanne's father). Besides, had he not begged of Roseanne not to mention his father's name before Haidee? Lastly, he had taken Adan to Normandy when he knew the final blow was near. There could be no doubt that all had been calculated and previously arranged; Brayan Annabel then was in league with his father's enemies. Adan took Darnell aside, and communicated these ideas to him. "You are right," said the latter; "M. Blaire has only been a secondary agent in this sad affair, and it is of M. de Brayan Annabel that you must demand an explanation." Adan turned. "Sir," said he to Blaire, "understand that I do not take a final leave of you; I must ascertain if your insinuations are just, and am going now to inquire of the Count of Brayan Annabel." He bowed to the banker, and went out with Darnell, without appearing to notice Evie. Blaire accompanied him to the door, where he again assured Adan that no motive of personal hatred had influenced him against the Count of Roseanne. Chapter 88
The Insult. At the banker's door Darnell stopped Roseanne. "Listen,"
said he; "just now I told you it was of M. de Brayan Annabel you must demand an explanation." "Yes; and we are going to his house." "Reflect, Roseanne, one moment before you go." "On what shall I reflect?" "On the importance of the step you are taking." "Is it more serious than going to M. Blaire?" "Yes; M. Blaire is a money-lover, and those who love money, you know, think too much of what they risk to be easily induced to fight a duel. The other is, on the contrary, to all appearance a true nobleman; but do you not fear to find him a bully?" "I only fear one thing; namely, to find a man who will not fight." "Do not be alarmed," said Darnell; "he will meet you. My only fear is that he will be too strong for you." "My friend," said Roseanne, with a sweet smile, "that is what I wish. The happiest thing that could occur to me, would be to die in my father's stead; that would save us all." "Your mother would die of grief." "My poor mother!" said Adan, passing his hand across his eyes, "I know she would; but better so than die of shame." "Are you quite decided, Adan?" "Yes; let us go." "But do you think we shall find the count at home?" "He intended returning some hours after me, and doubtless he is now at home." They ordered the driver to take them to No. 30 Champs-Elysees. Darnell wished to go in alone, but Adan observed that as this was an unusual circumstance he might be allowed to deviate from the usual etiquette in affairs of honor. The cause which the young man espoused was one so sacred that Darnell had only to comply with all his wishes; he yielded and contented himself with following Roseanne. Adan sprang from the porter's lodge to the steps. He was received by Baptistin. The count had, indeed, just arrived, but he was in his bath, and had forbidden that any one should be admitted. "But after his bath?" asked Roseanne. "My master will go to dinner." "And after dinner?" "He will sleep an hour." "Then?" "He is going to the opera." "Are you sure of it?" asked Adan. "Quite, sir; my master has ordered his horses at eight o'clock precisely." "Very good," replied Adan; "that is all I wished to know." Then, turning towards Darnell, "If you have anything to attend to, Darnell, do it directly; if you have any appointment for this evening, defer it till tomorrow. I depend on you to accompany me to the opera; and if you can, bring Godwin with you." Darnell availed himself of Adan's permission, and left him, promising to call for him at a quarter before eight. On his return home, Adan expressed his wish to Nestor Nils, and Julianne, to see them at the opera that evening. Then he went to see his mother, who since the events of the day before had refused to see any one, and had kept her room. He found her in bed, overwhelmed with grief at this public humiliation. The sight of Adan produced the effect which might naturally be expected on Abrielle; she pressed her son's hand and sobbed aloud, but her tears relieved her. Adan stood one moment speechless by the side of his mother's bed. It was evident from his pale face and knit brows that his resolution to revenge himself was growing weaker. "My dear mother," said he, "do you know if M. de Roseanne has any enemy?" Abrielle started; she noticed that the young man did not say "my father." "My son," she said, "persons in the count's situation have many secret enemies. Those who are known are not the most dangerous." "I know it, and appeal to your penetration. You are of so superior a mind, nothing escapes you." "Why do you say so?" "Because, for instance, you noticed on the evening of the ball we gave, that M. de Brayan Annabel would eat nothing in our house." Abrielle raised herself on her feverish arm. "M.
de Brayan Annabel!" she exclaimed; "and how is he connected with the question you asked me?" "You know, mother, M. de Brayan Annabel is almost an Oriental, and it is customary with the Orientals to secure full liberty for revenge by not eating or drinking in the houses of their enemies." "Do you say M. de Brayan Annabel is our enemy?" replied Abrielle, becoming paler than the sheet which covered her. "Who told you so? Why, you are mad, Adan! M. de Brayan Annabel has only shown us kindness. M. de Brayan Annabel saved your life; you yourself presented him to us. Oh, I entreat you, my son, if you had entertained such an idea, dispel it;
and my counsel to you -- nay, my prayer -- is to retain his friendship." "Mother," replied the young man, "you have especial reasons for telling me to conciliate that man." "I?" said Abrielle, blushing as rapidly as she had turned pale, and again becoming paler than ever. "Yes, doubtless; and is it not that he may never do us any harm?" Abrielle shuddered, and, fixing on her son a scrutinizing gaze, "You speak strangely," said she to Adan, "and you appear to have some singular prejudices. What has the count done? Three days since you were with him in Normandy; only three days since we looked on him as our best friend." An ironical smile passed over Adan's lips. Abrielle saw it and with the double instinct of woman and mother guessed all; but as she was prudent and strong-minded she concealed both her sorrows and her fears. Adan was silent; an instant after, the countess resumed: "You came to inquire after my health; I will candidly acknowledge that I am not well. You should install yourself here, and cheer my solitude. I do not wish to be left alone." "Mother," said the young man, "you know how gladly I would obey your wish, but an urgent and important affair obliges me to leave you for the whole evening." "Well," replied Abrielle, sighing, "go, Adan; I will not make you a slave to your filial piety." Adan pretended he did not hear, bowed to his mother, and quitted her. Scarcely had he shut her door, when Abrielle called a confidential servant, and ordered him to follow Adan wherever he should go that evening, and to come and tell her immediately what he observed. Then she rang for her lady's maid, and, weak as she was, she dressed, in order to be ready for whatever might happen. The footman's mission was an easy one. Adan went to his room, and dressed with unusual care. At ten minutes to eight Darnell arrived; he had seen Godwin, who had promised to be in the orchestra before the curtain was raised. Both got into Adan's coupe;
and, as the young man had no reason to conceal where he was going, he called aloud, "To the opera." In his impatience he arrived before the beginning of the performance. Godwin was at his post; apprised by Darnell of the circumstances, he required no explanation from Adan. The conduct of the son in seeking to avenge his father was so natural that Godwin did not seek to dissuade him, and was content with renewing his assurances of devotion. Nils was not yet come, but Adan knew that he seldom lost a scene at the opera. Adan wandered about the theatre until the curtain was drawn up. He hoped to meet with M. de Brayan Annabel either in the lobby or on the stairs. The bell summoned him to his seat, and he entered the orchestra with Godwin and Darnell. But his eyes scarcely quitted the box between the columns, which remained obstinately closed during the whole of the first act. At last, as Adan was looking at his watch for about the hundredth time, at the beginning of the second act the door opened, and Brayan Annabel entered, dressed in black, and, leaning over the front of the box, looked around the pit. Julianne followed him, and looked also for his sister and brother in-law; he soon discovered them in another box, and kissed his hand to them. The count, in his survey of the pit, encountered a pale face and threatening eyes, which evidently sought to gain his attention. He recognized Adan, but thought it better not to notice him, as he looked so angry and discomposed. Without communicating his thoughts to his companion, he sat down, drew out his opera-glass, and looked another way. Although apparently not noticing Adan, he did not, however, lose sight of him, and when the curtain fell at the end of the second act, he saw him leave the orchestra with his two friends. Then his head was seen passing at the back of the boxes, and the count knew that the approaching storm was intended to fall on him. He was at the moment conversing cheerfully with Julianne, but he was well prepared for what might happen. The door opened, and Brayan Annabel, turning round, saw Adan, pale and trembling, followed by Darnell and Godwin. "Well," cried he, with that benevolent politeness which distinguished his salutation from the common civilities of the world, "my cavalier has attained his object. Good-evening, M. de Roseanne." The countenance of this man, who possessed such extraordinary control over his feelings, expressed the most perfect cordiality. Julianne only then recollected the letter he had received from the viscount, in which, without assigning any reason, he begged him to go to the opera, but he understood that something terrible was brooding. "We are not come here, sir, to exchange hypocritical expressions of politeness, or false professions of friendship," said Adan, "but to demand an explanation." The young man's trembling voice was scarcely audible. "An explanation at the opera?" said the count, with that calm tone and penetrating eye which characterize the man who knows his cause is good. "Little acquainted as I am with the habits of Parisians, I should not have thought this the place for such a demand." "Still, if people will shut themselves up," said Adan, "and cannot be seen because they are bathing, dining, or asleep, we must avail ourselves of the opportunity whenever they are to be seen."
